subject: Could be this a different (and correct) way to apply multi season models?

messages.author: 564e5c2fe0c2d390
messages.subject: Could be this a different (and correct) way to apply multi season models?
parts:
Hi all,

First, I want to thank all the experienced people who kindly provide guidelnes to new modelers, your help is priceless for all of us.

I'm analyzing a camera trap data set from years 2013, 2015 and 2017, with very sparse data (some sites were sampled only in particular years, and with varying sampling period during each year). The cameras were active many months each year (almost all year round in some cases), and the area is highly seasonal, with heavy snowfall in winter months, while dry and hot in summer (it is located in a mountain range in mediterranean ecosystem in central Chile). Some species (mainly a large ungulate) show to migrate from higher altitude sites to lower sites towards winter months, escaping from snow coverage. I used months as seasons, instead of years as normally used, for modeling relative abundance and immigration/apparent survival rates of this ungulate in the study area towards winter. I fitted open N-mixture models using monthly dynamic covariates as snow coverage or changes in NDVI. Is this approach correct? my sampling units (where cameras were located) represent the large ungulate home range observed in one month. 

The years were stacked and used as covariate as I wanted to use as much data as I could. I also used 5 months of sampling from late summer days to winter months. I received some criticism and skepticism from my thesis comitee as they couldn't tell if stacking data and using months as seasons was right. I'd think it is, as I see it, only biological meaning changes, as recruitment parameter should be interpreted only as immigration, because no birth could occur during the sampling period (births only occur on spring months). I think I do not violate the assumption of closure (I account for monthly home range size of the species), and seasons have equal time interval (30 days). I should mention that I divided each month in three 10-day occasions of camera sampling, and counted total photographs of the species (independent events of 30minutes between photograph) for each 10-day occasion (that's why it should be interpreted as relative abundance).

I hope I was clear enough with the explanation and I wish someone can give his impression about this approach. What am I doing wrong? 

Thanks for reading!,

José Infante.
